en: *Jianwen Lu* (Record of What Was Seen and Heard), by the Śramaṇa Zhixu of Ancient Wu. A casual note:

There was once a civil examination candidate in the region of Chu whose heart and conduct were upright. It happened that the seventh hall of the Netherworld was vacant, and the Supreme Emperor issued a decree.

I temporarily presided over them. Every few days, I would enter the underworld to attend to affairs; however, I merely sat upright to examine the ledgers and did not trouble myself with signing or issuing judgments.
Yet, according to the past deeds of those before me, their destinies diverged into either sin or merit.

Whenever I saw someone ascending the mountain of knives or the forest of swords, I would repeatedly order my attendants to rescue them; yet the more they were rescued, the higher they climbed, until in the end none could be pulled back. (1)
One day, while examining the registers, he saw that his wife had an entry for one offense: she had stolen a neighbor’s chicken. It weighed one *jin* and twelve *liang*, including its feathers;

he had even broken it open to identify it. Upon returning to the living world, he interrogated his wife about it. She still continued to prevaricate and deny it, so he confronted her with what he had seen in the netherworld.
Thereupon, she confessed, saying, "The neighbor's chicken was eating some food left out to dry, and I accidentally struck it by mistake."

He had caused the chicken to die, but fearing the harsh reproaches of his neighbor’s wife, he had kept it hidden and not yet disposed of it. He then took it out and weighed it; the weight was exactly as before. They looked at each other in astonishment.
He subsequently paid the price of the dead chicken as compensation to the neighbor.

Not long after, he entered the underworld again and examined his previous ledger; the fold-marks remained as they were, yet the record of his offense had vanished without a trace. (Recorded by the Chan practitioner Yangzhi of Jiangxi)
(Thus it was said).
Feng Quan, the provincial examination head (Jieyuan) of Zhejiang during the Yimao cycle, entered the capital of Yan for the metropolitan examination.

There was an elderly man who had only two daughters; seeing that Feng was a renowned scholar, he bowed and entrusted them to him. When Feng failed the examination and returned home, he brought them with him to Yangzhou.
In the prefecture, [Feng] Quan secretly sold them to a brothel. When the matchmaker came to collect the two women, they reviled him, accusing him of deception.
The matchmaker produced Quan’s handwritten contract and showed it to them; the two women wept in terror and subsequently threw themselves into the water and died.
That night, Quan’s wife dreamed that two women with disheveled hair entered through a drainage ditch, followed by a ghost holding a tiger-head plaque upon which was written: "Quickly seize Feng."
When Quan heard these four words, he was startled and awakened. Before long, Quan returned home in safety. His wife received him with great joy.

Quan asked, "I have failed my examination; for what reason are you so exceedingly joyful? His wife remained silent and did not speak. When he pressed her repeatedly for an answer, she then recounted her previous dream.
Just as Quan was walking up and down on the upper floor of the tower, having heard the end of her account of the dream, his body began to tremble violently, and he fell from the tower.

Blood flowed from his seven apertures as he collapsed unconscious upon the ground. His family members hurriedly supported him and called for him to wake up. He then recounted in detail the matter of his betrayal;
having finished speaking, he died (as told by a man from Jiaxing on board the boat).
Lu Gu, a student at the Confucian academy of Suzhou, whose courtesy name was Jianfu, formerly studied under masters such as Han Hui and Zhan Ming.
Later, he specialized in Chan Buddhism and attained significant insights; he subsequently became even more profound and tranquil.

At the end of the year of Gengwu, while traveling by small boat on a mission, he suddenly encountered six men from a grain boat who asked to board his vessel. The boat then capsized, and all six men...
"I am well. Gu was ultimately drowned. His family members claimed that his practice lacked efficacy. Thereupon, [the deity] appeared in a dream and said:
'In a previous life, I once harmed these six people through a certain means. I am now repaying my past debt; it is not the fault of your practice.'"
If one does not practice cultivation, the retribution shall be even more severe.
The lay practitioner Cai Tanru of Mount Xi in Dongting had a most virtuous wife who observed the fasts, recited the Buddha’s name, released living beings, and lit lamps;
she secretly performed these various meritorious deeds without seeking recognition from others. When her illness became critical, she said to Tanru, "Death is certainly not something to be feared."
He requested that a day be chosen. However, the worldly people held a common view, saying that for a practitioner to die on an inauspicious day would be inconvenient.

He thus asked, "Please choose a day for me. Will tomorrow be auspicious? The answer was, "It will not be auspicious. He then asked, "Will the following day be auspicious? The answer was, "That too will not be auspicious."
He then said, "I cannot wait any longer. Is today auspicious? The reply was, "Today is quite auspicious.
Thereupon, he ordered water to be brought for bathing, gathered his relatives and friends to recite the Buddha's name, sat upright with palms joined, and passed away.
On the shores of Lake Tai in Wujiang, there was an old man. Throughout his life, he took pleasure solely in reciting the Buddha’s name and practicing the release of living beings;
he knew nothing else. Whenever he traveled, he would pick up snails and clams from the shore and place them in the water, regardless of how busy he might be.

On ordinary days, whenever he encountered living creatures, he would immediately take off his clothes, cut out his own flesh to buy them their freedom, never once showing weariness or indolence. One day, he suddenly said:
His family said, "I am about to pass away in the west; you may gather your relatives and friends to see me off. Thereupon, he assembled the multitude to recite the Buddha's name.
He sat peacefully until his passing, and a wondrous fragrance lingered for a night without dispersing (as told by Master Jiankong of Wujiang).
In the northern gate of Hangzhou, Luo Si was casting a mirror for a statue of Mahākaruṇika. An old woman assisted him with a small mirror;
Luo, appreciating its antiquity, kept it. When first cast, the mirror was only formed as four sides; when cast a second time, it was only formed as half a mirror.
One of the three castings was missing a single hole; its size was exactly equal to that of the ancient mirror he had kept.
He then took out the mirror he had preserved and threw it into the furnace, saying: "If this casting succeeds, I shall perform repentance; if it does not succeed, it is not my fault."

The casting of the image was completed immediately. Thereupon, he again donated his wealth to perform rites of repentance (*pratikramaṇa*). Today, that mirror is currently enshrined at the altar for repentance at Yongqing Temple in Longju.
At the West Wangxiang Bridge on Mount Yang in Gusu, there lived a resident couple who, whenever the rice ripened, would invariably [perform offerings].
She would pluck ears of grain from her neighbor’s field to supplement her own. One day she died. Her parents, possessing a woman’s body, rebuked her bitterly, saying:
"You stole your neighbor’s grain; therefore, the underworld authorities have compelled me to pluck ears from my own field to repay you."
Both his hands were wounded, and he could not endure the agony. "Why have you harmed me to such an extent? he cried.
Furthermore, there was a resident who grew vegetables; when a neighbor cut away an entire plot by severing it at the roots, he endured it without contesting the act.
The vegetables grew back from their roots and flourished twice as much as usual. On the following night, the neighbor again cut down another plot;
the man could no longer endure it and cursed him bitterly. However, the vegetable roots remaining in that plot were so numerous that they eventually withered and rotted away, never to grow again.
Furthermore, another resident demanded the repayment of a debt. The debtor, finding him too pressing, struck back at him with his mouth.
The creditor, harboring resentment, said: "How can you owe me goods and yet refuse to repay me? You shall surely be bitten by a venomous snake.
Before long, he suffered from jaundice and remained bedridden for over a year. When the debtor heard that his illness was grave, he thought to himself:
"Originally, I had no intention of betraying him; it was because his conduct was so wicked that I merely feigned a conflict with him.
Now that I hear he is ill, I shall repay him. Thereupon, he prepared one copy [of a scripture], one blade, and four boxes of gifts to go and apologize.
The man was exceedingly pleased and invited him to drink together. While intoxicated, he suddenly vomited up a snake, and his illness was immediately cured.

A commoner in Hangzhou possessed several mu of fields whose boundaries lay within the lands of the official Zhu. Zhu used his power and influence to forcibly seize them, and the man had no one to whom he could appeal.
He swore that in a future life he would become a snake to sting him, and subsequently fell gravely ill. He instructed a craftsman to build a coffin with a single hole left in it.

When the craftsman asked for the reason, the man explained the situation, and the craftsman reported this to Zhu. Zhu was filled with remorse and realization; he sent a carriage to fetch the man to his home.
He returned the deed to his field and provided him with funds for medical care. The man wept with gratitude and immediately spat out a snake;
it sprang up and ran away, returning to its home (the lay practitioner Wang Yuanjian personally knew this event).
In Hangzhou, there was a man named Xu Xingsu. His wife had suffered from a grave illness for over three years, and her condition was such that death seemed certain.

One night, she dreamed that a mass of multicolored clouds bore a Bodhisattva to her courtyard; she woke up filled with joy and wonder. It happened that at that time, the Great Master Yunqi had arrived in the city.
Xu led his entire family to earnestly request the Master’s presence. The Master instructed them to first establish a ritual site for sutra recitation and repentance for four days.
On the final day, he went there; the sick man felt as if he were seeing things in a dream and was subsequently cured.

At the beginning of the Tianqi era, mulberry leaves were extremely expensive in Wujiang. A resident who raised silkworms in several baskets calculated that the profit from the cocoons would not exceed the profit from selling the leaves;
he therefore buried the silkworms, loaded the leaves onto a cart, and traveled to Huzhou to sell them.
As their boat passed Lake Tai, a large carp leaped into the vessel. The man took it and hid it in the forward cabin.
Upon arriving at Ye-dian, the host saw blood on the leaves and questioned him as to the cause. He replied, "This is the blood of this fish."
The fish were still in the fore-cabin. When they took one up to examine it, it was clearly a human head. They were all struck with terror and pressed him for an explanation.
He replied, "Truly there is no other reason. I personally buried silkworms and sold their leaves, wishing only to reap greater profit.
Consequently, he went with the others to the place where the silkworms had been buried; when they dug into the earth and looked, they found another corpse, which matched the head.
The evidence was consistent; the case was reported to the authorities, and in the end, he was sentenced to death. Alas!

When one’s karma acts as a silkworm, one cannot escape the suffering of being boiled in a cocoon—this is already most cruel. How much more so when, for the sake of a meager profit, one buries them alive and prevents them from completing even a single lifetime?
Where is the human heart? It is no wonder that the retribution was so swift.
My maternal uncle, Jin Chicheng, was serving as the Governor of Ganzhou. Upon returning home from his audience with the Emperor, he contracted malaria during the summer.

While resting with his head on a small table, he fell into a light sleep and had a dream: officials and laborers of the government office were lined up to his left, while monastics in black robes were lined up to his right.
Then an old man spoke to him, saying, "You originally came from among the monastics; now you must turn back and return to this path."
"If you are able, it would still be possible for me to escort your aged mother; if you are not able, then your mother will instead have to escort you.
The uncle then thought, "My mother is already eighty-four years old; how could I allow her to escort me? He immediately replied, "I shall turn back.
Before his voice had even finished, the laborers dispersed. Thereupon, he followed the assembly of monastics as they chanted the *brahman* hymns.
Suddenly, a sense of solitude and desolation arose within me; I awoke from my dream with sorrow and regret. On another occasion, while he was at his mourning hut in Yangshan, he spoke of this to me.
However, because his official ambitions were so fervent, he remained in office at Ganzhou. Before long, he was promoted to the Military Commissioner of Yandong.
He returned home and died after being ill for three or four days. Thus, it ultimately caused his mother, over eighty years of age, to stand until her tear-filled eyes were nearly dried. Alas!
For a mere speck of a fly or the tip of a snail's horn, the human mind and will can become so deluded that they fail in both worldly and world-transcending dharmas.
This may serve as an eternal mirror for those on the path to the azure clouds.
On Nan-hao Street in Gusu, there was a man who regularly served as a subordinate official in the underworld. Every few days, he would go on duty at the front post.
A neighbor said to him, "Could you take me with you to the underworld for some recreation? The official replied, "I can.
You simply lie down quietly in your room and command your family not to open the door; I shall take you there and then escort you back. The neighbor—
As he had commanded, the subordinate immediately summoned his soul and brought it together with him to the front of the City God Temple in the prefectural seat.
He instructed the spirit to remain beneath the stone archway to wait, while he himself took the official documents and entered the inner courtyard.
After waiting for a long time, the neighbor grew weary and annoyed; he saw a large carriage pass from west to east, carrying four courtesans and two men. In the middle...
There was a courtesan with whom he had a prior intimacy. He beckoned her with his hand, and she boarded the carriage with him.
The slave left the temple to look for the neighbor but could not find him; he then questioned others nearby and learned that the neighbor had boarded the carriage and departed.
He returned in great haste to the gate of Fu’s residence, where he saw a resident who had recently given birth to seven small piglets, one of which belonged to the neighbor. With his hand—
He threw it; the pig fell dead and its soul suddenly vanished. Next, by the bank of a field, he saw a large red snake lying on its back.
He immediately realized it was a transformation by his neighbor, so he beat it to death, compressed its soul, and brought it back to his room.
Upon throwing it to revive it, he asked, "Did you find your journey through the underworld to be agreeable? It replied, "When you first placed me before the stone tablet in front of the temple..."

Below the pavilion, I entered the temple and remained there for a long time without coming out. I was becoming weary and disenchanted when a former acquaintance, a courtesan, invited me out through the gate of the Fufu (傅) family.
We went together to a lodging where we ate, drank, and enjoyed ourselves. Suddenly, someone snatched my food and struck me on the neck.
Enraged, I went outside and lay down to rest. Then, I heard someone calling out: "Red snake! Red snake!"
He seized me with his hand, and I woke up in a start. "What pleasure is there in this? I asked. Lei laughed and told me the reason for it.
Huang Hongjiang personally heard this account and subsequently resolved to study the Way (Hongjiang was also a virtuous friend of mine during my lay years).
Zhuang Qixian of Quanzhou was the second-ranked graduate (bangyan) of the Gui-chou examination cycle. Being young and fond of wine, he one day drank at Chengtian Temple;
after becoming intoxicated, he went to the repository of the Tripitaka and saw a Dharma Master lecturing on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* (Da Foding Jing).

He then flew into a great rage, seized the scriptures from the table and threw them to the ground, treading upon them with his feet. He further toppled a statue of Vajrapāṇi to the floor. Several months later...

He kicked a servant with his foot, but by mistake it struck a pillar, causing his toes to split open and form a strange ulcer. The swelling gradually spread to his entire body, and the agony became extraordinary.
He was then seen being interrogated and rebuked by Vaiśravaṇa before he died.

Zhang Han-chong of Quanzhou was a jinshi graduate of the Bingchen year. While serving as the Magistrate of Jintan, one day as he sat upon the magistrate’s bench about to be summoned to the capital, a monk suddenly approached the official hall and said:
"I and you were spiritual companions in a previous life. Seeing that you face hardship, I have come specifically to save you.
You should resign your office and enter the mountains together to study the Way; not only will this spare you from calamity," [but it will also lead to great benefit].

Furthermore, [Seng]zhi claimed he had transcended birth and death. Zhang considered this to be a fabrication. Sengzhi then proceeded to point out several instances from his youth, all of which were unknown to his wife and children.
Zhang was then struck with awe and wished to act according to his words, but was ultimately thwarted by his wife and children.

Sengzhi soon departed; Zhang went to the capital for the official examination. Just as he reached the city gates, a strange abscess suddenly broke out on his leg, such that it could not even fit inside his boot.
He was able to escape. He cut up his boots to prepare a remedy, but it did not heal him and he died.
Xu Zhaoxin of Jinjiang, a licentiate in the Wumu year, went to Funing Prefecture to visit his former tutor.

He happened to pass by a nunnery and became infatuated with a young nun; he then used his official authority to intimidate her and forcibly defiled her. The following day, she suddenly bit herself [to death].
His tongue was severed twice, and he died.
Wang, a man from Jinjiang, was renowned among the students for his literary talent. Once, while carrying wine to drink at Chengtian Temple, he entered the Hall of the Tripitaka.
He saw a young novice śrāmaṇera sitting upright reading a sutra and forcibly compelled him to drink wine; the śrāmaṇera refused.
He then seized and embraced him, mocking and harassing him. Upon returning home three days later, he suddenly struck his own mouth with his palm and cursed himself.
His family did not understand what this meant, but after half a day, he bit off his tongue and died.
Yang Gong, a student of the provincial registry from Xiaofeng County, owned eight matchlocks and several hunting dogs, which he used to injure and kill living beings wherever he went.
One day, while intending to go to his estate to harvest rice, the entire family had a dream in which it was said: "The karma created over ten years has reached its point;
the retribution for evil deeds is now imminent. Yang did not believe this and, taking his gun with him, arrived at the estate. There he saw a wild pheasant and shot it with his gun.
It struck his own head by mistake; his skull was shattered, and he died.
A daughter of the Xu family in Quanzhou, named Sanjie, was sixteen years old and unmarried when she suddenly fell ill.
Her parents sought a physician for her, but the girl wept and said to them, "I am certain to die; there is no need for a physician. For in my previous life, I was..."
"A woman from such-and-such a family had a maidservant whom her husband favored. Out of jealousy, I plotted to kill her. Now she is lodging a complaint with the officials of the underworld;
I must go there to repay her for it—I cannot escape. On the following day, she died.

There was a woman of the Xu clan from Quanzhou named Tiejie. After she married, she bore several children; during her pregnancies, she frequently ate chicken, and the number of chickens she had killed was considerable.
Later, while again in labor, she fell ill and saw a flock of chickens demanding her life before she died.
There was a man named Yao of Jinjiang. His cousin, Xu Xiaowu, because of the famine, donated one hundred taels of gold to provide relief for the hungry and entrusted Yao with managing the affair.
Yao concealed ten or more taels to enrich himself. A few days later, he fell ill and cursed himself, saying:
"Xu entrusted you to relieve the hunger of others; how could you embezzle and hide [the funds], causing so many to die of starvation? Now I shall take your life as retribution. Thereupon—
He died. Later, his two younger sons also perished of starvation.
A daughter of the Xu family in Quanzhou, named Xiying, was seven years old when she contracted the disease of *ganji* (intestinal consumption) and was on the verge of death.

Her father, Yu Hai, struck the sounding stone and recited the Buddha’s name aloud to send her off. Although her breath had ceased, she suddenly revived. Consequently, he invited a nun to attend to her.
The monks recited one hundred and twenty fascicles of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. The girl became peaceful and appeared as if free from illness;
the entire family believed her recovery was complete. However, the girl alone said to her father, "Child, please grant me a few more days so that I may finish listening to the sutra before departing.
Once the sutra was finished, she passed away.
In Quanzhou, there was a man surnamed Lai whose family was immensely wealthy. He took pleasure in taking life;

he had excavated a small pond within his home, enclosing it from top to bottom with an iron net, where he kept eels, loach, fish, and turtles to provide for his occasional meals. Later, he fell ill and was on the verge of death. His sons were gathered in a row before his bed when they suddenly could not see him.

They searched everywhere but could not find him, until finally they saw him— *Note: The text provided ends abruptly. The narrative typically continues with the deceased appearing as a hungry ghost or spirit to warn his children of the karmic consequences of his actions.*
He had already died within the iron fence of the small pond.
In Jinjiang, there was a ruffian whose name has been forgotten; he constantly made a profession of killing dogs.
Along the roadside ditches near the gates of Xingquan Dao, he slaughtered countless dogs. Suddenly one day, he crouched by the side of a ditch and began barking like a dog for several days.
He then died.
During the reign of Emperor Shenzong, there was a man from the southern region named Wang Wanzuo who served as a river patrol commander.

He was exceptionally upright and incorruptible in office, yet his temperament was quite stern and impetuous; under his beatings and punishments, many lost their lives. Suddenly he fell ill, and ghosts of the wronged appeared within his yamen.
For several hundred paces around, there were cries of lamentation. His colleagues, the various Censors, went to inquire about it; there was no one who had not seen or heard [the commotion].
At the fifth watch, the King finally did not rise.
In the mountains of Nanan County, there was a resident who rose at night and saw a man from a neighboring house driving another man into his gate.
The man refused to enter and said, "I owe him only three cents; how can I be made to enter so readily?"
The driver struck it with his staff, and it entered. The residents found this quite strange and inquired about it the following morning;

they discovered that a pig had already been born in a neighboring house. The people further suspected that the value of the pig was not merely three *fen*. Before long, the pig fell into a latrine and died.
Ultimately, there was one person who purchased it for three *fen* of silver, and the people’s doubts were finally resolved.
Shi Ziqian of Lingyan Temple in Xiaofeng was a lay friend named Lao Zhenyu before he entered the monastic order.
A native of Jiangyou, he sold eel noodles at Didipu Beach and annually slaughtered several thousand pounds of eels. Later, he moved his residence to Deqing County.
He continued to practice his former occupation. One day, while boiling eels in boiling water, someone grabbed his hand;
he was unable to cover the pot, and the eels, leaping up with the bubbling broth, swarmed around his face, biting him firmly and refusing to let go. Zhenyu wailed and lamented in a myriad of ways.
Only after a short while did the eels die, and he was finally released. Less than ten days later, Zhenyu himself passed away.

Shi Xingjie’s secular surname was Wan. He had a younger brother named Wanqi, who pursued no other occupation but specialized in using ropes to strangle various birds, pheasants, foxes, hares, dogs, and the like.
Although Shi repeatedly exhorted him to change his profession, he would not comply for more than ten years.
Later, one night while lying on his bed, he wrapped his neck with a rotten rope; no one knew of it. When he did not rise the following morning, they finally discovered it.
He opened the door and looked inside; [the dog] had already died of itself.
During the reign of Emperor Shenzong, Zhou Kongjiao, the Provincial Inspector of Yingtian, was passing through his home on his way to take up his new post as a Vice Minister.
Several subordinate officials were all composing letters and dispatching servants to offer thanks for his recommendation. The servant waited at his gate but had not yet gained entry. Immediately—
Tong suddenly saw a messenger holding a single sheet of paper with the five characters "Your humble servant Shi Xing bows" written on a red slip.
The gatekeeper hurriedly announced his arrival. As Zhou was sitting in meditation, he saw this and was greatly alarmed. Shortly thereafter, both the note and the messenger vanished.
Zhou’s illness then became critical; as his descendants stood surrounding him, he again saw more than thirty people with their heads wrapped in white cloth.
He burst into the bedroom and rebuked them; they each held their own heads in their hands to show him, for they were actually headless ghosts.

Zhou subsequently died. Upon investigating the cause, it was found that when Shi Xiang served as Minister of War, Zhou had been an Imperial Censor who impeached him, leading to his imprisonment and sentencing to death.
Furthermore, more than thirty others were those who had been mistakenly executed during Zhou's tenure as Provincial Governor due to false reports regarding bandits.
There was a resident in Songmen卫 (Wèi) of Taizhou Prefecture who, in the fifth month of the Xīnmèi year of the Chóngzhēn era,
stole a sandalwood statue of the Great Being (Bodhisattva). He traveled to Tiāntái County intending to sell it to the local scholar-official Zhāng Dàsù, who agreed to purchase it.
The price was set at six taels of gold. The commoner found this too little and intended to split the image in half to sell it as incense.
At that time, a police officer dreamed one night of a woman pleading for help in her distress. As his own wife had died not long before, he suspected she was seeking a funeral offering.
He went to the Ximen shop to purchase sacrificial offerings. Suddenly, he heard the sound of an image being split open inside the shop.

He hurried in to look and was suddenly enlightened by his previous dream. Consequently, he was seized and brought before the local magistrate. That magistrate had also received a dream on the night prior; thus, he subjected him to rigorous interrogation.
The man confessed that he had stolen it from Songmen and immediately reported this to the district magistrate, who returned the image [to its rightful owner].
He repaired and made offerings at the residence of Zhang; however, before long, that man died in prison.
At Gaoming Temple, the novice monk Yuehong was in charge of the storehouse.

He embezzled funds from the community without restraint, frequently preparing food and drink privately within the storehouse to enjoy exclusively with his own faction, and even stealing the temple’s standing provisions of beans and rice for his personal use.
It had been used for barely a year when, on the night of New Year’s Day, he dreamed that Lord Guan cut off his tongue and took it away.

On the fourth day, he fell gravely ill and was on the verge of death. Terrified and with no place to turn, he sold all his clothing and bedding to solicit the community for repentance and took leave of the treasury office.
Only then did his illness gradually subside.
At Gaoming Temple, there was another śrāmaṇera named Linghao who had never observed the precepts.

The Venerable Rui Guang led a group of pure practitioners, each contributing their own funds, to establish a period for the Great Compassion Repentance; Linghao also participated. While he was still in the midst of this period, he continued to engage in improper conduct.
Consequently, he dreamed that Lord Guan severed his head and took it away. The following day, he vomited blood incessantly and fell gravely ill.
He died after several months.
Shi Shixiang of Foji Temple left home to become a monk in his middle years; he was solely diligent in practicing asceticism and made it his business to oversee the monastery’s permanent assets.
He would recite the Buddha’s name while performing his duties, and whatever he obtained, he gave away immediately without keeping any surplus wealth. He did not contend with others, nor...
He never showed an angry countenance. One day in the autumn of the Ren-shen year, he suddenly said to others, "I shall depart for the West tomorrow.
He then borrowed a sitting niche from an old man of Yunqi. On the following day, he bathed and shaved his hair; before the shaving was even finished, he passed away while seated.
Shi Liaokong of Longxi Hermitage in Anji Prefecture invited the Dharma Master Juehai to lecture on the *Lotus Sūtra*.
Because the ceremonies for welcoming and seeing him off were so grand, the local villagers became envious. They enticed a reckless man surnamed Mo to strike the Dharma Master with a single punch.

The assembly of monks, being greatly incensed, beat him severely until Mo was on the verge of death. Taking advantage of this opportunity, the villagers intended to frame the hermitage by reporting the matter to the authorities.
Upon examination, his body showed no minor injuries, yet his appetite for food was even more diminished than before. The official was thus unable to determine a crime.

When he was taken back to his secular residence by carriage, his entire body was found to be covered in wounds; both eating and drinking had ceased. Half a year later, pus and blood were still flowing from beneath his ribs.
It took a long time before he recovered. Thus, one may believe that the power of the *saṃghārāma* to protect the Dharma is inconceivable. Recorded on a spring day in the Guiyou year.
In the hermitage, Shi Yinkong personally recounted this.
During the reign of Emperor Shizong, the local gentry of Wucheng, Lu Feng, coveted the superior geomantic features of the West Lake Temple on Mount Dongting.

They plotted with all their might to seize and devour [the temple], but because the two local families, the Zou and the Lu, were fiercely opposed to one another and engaged in bitter litigation, they did not achieve their purpose.
Consequently, they set fire to the main hall. Within the hall was an ancient sandalwood statue of Avalokiteśvara; as it burned, a fragrant scent wafted far and wide.

Subsequently, the instigator contracted a strange illness from which his entire body became covered in itching sores. They poured boiling water over him until he was completely rotted away before he died. As for those who conspired with him...
People alike receive retribution for their evil deeds.
During the Ming Dynasty, the local gentry of Wu City, Mao Kan, encroached upon Tianchi Temple to build a tomb; he intended to demolish the stone Buddha hall to serve as his burial pit.
On a clear and bright day, a violent thunderbolt suddenly struck, shattering the ceremonial archway (paipiao). Terrified, Kan consequently refrained from destroying it.
The Palace remained, with one or two monks staying there to maintain the incense offerings; however, the great temple had already fallen into ruin.
In that year, the children, grandchildren, and daughters-in-law all died, and subsequently, the lineage was completely extinguished.
In Fengqiao, there was a wealthy commoner who had long been a man of depraved character.

Fearing that he might be investigated by the Provincial Surveillance Commission (An Yuan), he feigned a virtuous appearance, holding prayer beads and reciting the Buddha’s name, abstaining from alcohol, and breaking his gambling tokens. His various evil associates also unanimously followed his example of conversion and hailed him as their teacher;
yet in reality, he continued to act unlawfully in private and committed many evils. However, all the prophecies regarding fortune and calamity he uttered were entirely efficacious.
His gains and offerings flourished daily for over a year. Suddenly, he thought to himself: "I originally lacked a sincere heart in my practice, yet I still received such favorable rewards.
This proves that the Buddha-dharma is not in vain. Consequently, he resolved to cultivate a sincere heart and sought out a good teacher. He received the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts.
Thereafter, the prophecies regarding his fortune and misfortune were not verified even once in a hundred instances. His gains and offerings consequently ceased, and he let out cries of resentment.

He said, "In the past, I practiced with deceit and hypocrisy, yet I received abundant offerings and support. Now that I study the Way with a sincere heart, I encounter even more setbacks and hardships.
Does the Buddha-dharma truly have any practical efficacy? Distressed, he fell into a light sleep and saw someone say to him, "Do not resent me.
In the past, you practiced deception, falsehood, and empty talk regarding fortune and calamity; we were thus able to assist one another."
"Help! Now that you have turned from the heterodox back to the orthodox, we can no longer associate with you;
this is why you feel so desolate. Shi Cihan was strolling by a wild pond with Liu Zhan when he saw two leeches that gradually transformed into dragonflies.
When he reached the third pool, Lu Zhan blocked it with grass; he blocked it three times in succession. Suddenly, the creature transformed into a centipede.
Layman Lu Zhan-yuan of Wu-cheng went to the home of Wu Feng-lin on East Mountain in Dong-ting, where his family was preparing for him.
A vegetarian offering was being prepared. Lady Wu, who was then ninety-four years of age, happened to go down to the kitchen and asked, "Why are you preparing this vegetarian offering?
The maidservant replied, "To invite Master Lu. She further asked, "How old is Master Lu? The maidservant replied, "He is fifty-four.
The lady sighed in amazement and said, "At fifty-four, he has already begun to consume only vegetarian food; I am ninety-four!"

"I have not yet severed my attachment to worldly ties. From this day forward, I shall forever sever them. His sons and daughters-in-law tried to dissuade him with all their might, but he would not listen.
He continued to prepare incense and candles, requesting the layman Lu to serve as his witness.
Three years later, during the twelfth lunar month, he suddenly said to his son, "Invite Master Lu here for me. The son was surprised and asked the reason. He replied, "I am about to travel far away."
The son asked where she was going. She replied, "Child, why are you so foolish? I am already ninety-seven years old; how could I not depart?
She then gathered all her descendants to bid them farewell and chose the following day to leave. On that next day, it snowed heavily, so she said, "Wait until the weather clears before we go.
The next day, when he again asked if the weather was clear, the maidservant falsely replied, "Today the snow is even heavier."
He then said, "Let us wait for the weather to clear. Before long, he saw the sunlight shining into the room. He then said, "You have deceived me;

quickly fetch my clean robes and bring some scented water. He immediately rose to wash his hair and change his clothes, then prostrated before the Buddha and offered distant salutations to the layman Zhanyuan.
Leaning upon his desk, he sat upright and commanded his family members to simultaneously recite the Buddha's name in low voices to see him off.
After a long time, when his daughter-in-law entered with tea and soup, she had already passed away.
His relative, Pan Fengyan of Shentang Lane in Gusu—whose nickname was "Rat"—had a nephew living in the countryside.
When Pan went to visit him, the nephew wished to slaughter a chicken for a meal, but Pan strenuously dissuaded him, and thus it was avoided. That night, he dreamed of his deceased daughter-in-law.
Xie said, "The rooster was my own body in a later life. Because I failed to show reverence to the Triple Gem, I fell into this animal form.

Relying on your compassionate power, Elder, I have been spared from the blade and the cutting board yesterday. Seven years ago, I once lost a hairpin inside a bamboo water-conduit; please have your wife retrieve it.
Once Cheng had regained consciousness, he immediately sought out the rooster and returned home with it; indeed, they found the old pin within the bamboo conduit.
Zan. Both husband and wife were deeply moved and inspired, and they left the household life together at Putuo Mountain. Later, the wife passed away while sitting in meditation;
the husband also met his end peacefully.
Zhou Zhihe of Suzhou made his living by selling medicine. He had a daughter-in-law who, after her death, entered the body of her younger sister and said:
He said, "I did not show reverence to the Triple Gem; as punishment, I have been reborn with the body of a dog. Daily I am beaten by the kitchen servants, and my suffering is beyond description.
I pray that you will quickly save me. His parents asked, "We performed the *Cibei Chanfa* (Compassionate Repentance) for your sake; did you receive any benefit?"
He replied, "It is precisely by relying on the power of repentance that you shall be delivered from this peril. Thereupon, his parents took a dog from the Zhou family and brought it home;
three days later, the dog died.
In Jinlong Creek in Gusu, there was a wife's younger brother who ran a noodle shop at Nanhao; while his family was beating a donkey, the donkey—
Suddenly, it spoke in human speech: "I owe your late master five pieces of gold;

therefore, I have come to work for you. How can you whip me? The family members were greatly alarmed and told their master. The master took his father’s old account books and examined them; indeed, he found a promissory note for five pieces of gold.
He then took the donkey forward and crushed the note, saying, "I have now released you. Thereupon, the donkey began to prance about.
He collapsed and died.
In Jinlong River, there was another cousin who lived at Hushu Pass. He had a son who was constantly ill.

Once, while father and son were lying down together, a ghost seized the father’s soul and brought him to the underworld. The official of the underworld rebuked him, saying: "You owe a debt to such-and-such a person."
"Gan! Why have you not returned for so long? His father replied, "I did not recognize you. He was then called out to identify himself; it was indeed his son.
He then recalled how, in a previous life, he had owed a debt. The official of the underworld commanded him, "You must quickly repay this to the Triple Gem on his behalf.
With a single word, he awoke; his son was there by his bedside as before, and his mind became doubly awakened. Later, [the father] acted on his behalf...

Regarding the matter of the physician Fuyan and others, once the full number of victims had been reached, the son passed away. His mother wept bitterly for him, but his father said, "There is no need to weep;
he was merely a collector of old debts. He then related the previous dream in detail. Consequently, they together observed the precepts and practiced the Way, and they remain so even to this day.
A public official from Wukang County in Huzhou Prefecture, whose name has been forgotten, encountered a man and two women on the road who followed behind him.

Upon arriving at the residence of the local scholar-official Luo, he saw the three enter directly into the Luo compound. Finding this strange, he waited until evening for them to emerge, but they did not come out.
He then questioned the gatekeeper and demanded that the men be produced; the gatekeeper, deeming his claims baseless and false, struck him repeatedly without ceasing.
They reported this to their master. The master understood their meaning and ordered each household to investigate the matter of livestock births.

Upon inspection, they found that three bulls had been born from a single cow—one being a mature bull and two being heifers. He immediately summoned the three men who had been assigned to oversee them;

the color of the three bulls was no different from the clothing colors of the three men they had seen. Only then did they realize that the three men had already become oxen. They further investigated their names, and all...
They were those who owed rice rents to the Luo family. Later, when the three oxen had grown large, their strength varied according to the magnitude of their debts:
those with heavy debts were strong, while those with light debts were weak; there was not even a hair’s breadth of discrepancy between them.
Within Loumen in Wucheng, there was a man surnamed Jiang who, from his youth, took pleasure in destroying divine images.
In the year Guiyou of the Chongzhen era, he tore down the fire-god shrine his father had built to use it as a gatehouse. He destroyed the divine images to use them as firewood for burning.
Suddenly, in winter, he suffered a headache. He ordered his family members to sound the *ra* and assemble the masses. Once the crowd had gathered, his eyeballs suddenly popped out and hung down.
Between his nostrils, he died and then revived; having revived, he died again. From his mouth, he uttered the various sufferings experienced in the underworld.
This continued for forty-two days before he finally passed away. There was no one in the entire city who did not see or hear of it.

A resident of Shuidong Township in Jing County, Ningguo Prefecture, whose name has been forgotten, habitually practiced virtue. He never missed a day in providing vegetarian feasts for monks or making offerings.

Once, he suddenly fell ill and passed away; upon arriving at the Netherworld, the King of the Dead examined his records and found that his allotted lifespan in the world of the living was not yet exhausted.
He was sent back. The man pleaded, saying, "I have suffered much; I do not wish to return. This he said two or three times. The king then asked, "What do you wish to become?
He replied, "I pray to be admitted into the ranks of the Sangha. The king was astonished and said, "How great is your merit that you hope for such a high station?
Calculating the power of your merit throughout your life, you could only serve as the head of a hundred households. The man again insisted on his request. If [the king] had not...
"You may well be a śramaṇa of renown and virtue; it would suffice for you to seek to become a fire-tending monk.
The king said, "Even the position of a fire-tending monk is not easily attained by the millions. How about I grant you a thousand households? The man again did not wish for this. The king said:
"If you truly wish to become a monk who burns incense, you must first return to the world of the living and cultivate merit with all your strength for the remainder of your natural life;

only then might such a hope be realized. Thereupon, the man revived and practiced meritorious deeds twice as much as before. He passed away several years later (as told by the Elder Kongru of Jiuhua).
During the reign of Emperor Shizong, there was a great counselor from Ying named Cheng Xi. He had a young son called Cheng Yi who, together with his cousins, was catching woodpigeons in a tree.
They had agreed that whoever climbed the tree would get two birds, while those remaining at the foot of the tree would get one.
When Yi climbed up and secured three pigeons, those at the base of the tree took them all away. Yi pursued them to reclaim his share, but they refused to return them. Consequently—
He seized them both and threw them down to kill them. That night, he dreamed that two men dressed in green came to arrest him, holding a placard that read:
"There is a matter of human life. Qi fled for about two li and hid inside the hall of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva. He saw the Bodhisattva sitting there with solemn dignity.
The two men in green also pursued him there. Qi appealed to the Bodhisattva, saying: "I have never killed anyone. Why [are you arresting me]?"
They seized me. Two green-clad attendants came out and showed me a warrant, saying, "The three magpies have informed us; you must now go with them to be dealt with.
Ziqi protested, saying, "Magpies are but small birds; why should they be worth my life? Moreover, I originally made an appointment with them."
"That man violated his agreement, which provoked my anger and led me to kill him; thus, the guilt does not rest on me alone.
The Great Being said, "Even if a pigeon were large enough to damage the grain seedlings, your crime in killing it would still be relatively minor.
Now, this one has just been born and has never committed a transgression; by all reason, you must repay its life for its taking yours. Moreover, although that man did violate his agreement,"
That you have been brought to this place of death is truly your own fault.

However, considering that you are young and not yet fully established, I have commanded two green-clad attendants to extend your limit until twelve years hence. On such-and-such a day and at such-and-such a time, they shall come again to pursue you.
The two maidservants in green robes dispersed as they had been commanded by the Great Being. Zhi also subsequently awoke.
Twelve years later, while Zhi was trading on the Songjiang River, he suddenly stood up by himself beneath the Xiuye Bridge and died.
Dafu Ying Cheng Xuanwei had one son named Ben-da, who studied Confucianism.

Having exhausted nearly all of his family’s assets, in the *xinsi* year of the Chongzhen era, he went to Suzhou with his paternal cousin Cheng Tianming to sell the ancestral house in their hometown to the latter’s nephew.
They received only several dozen taels of gold as the sale price, which was entirely pocketed by Tianming; they returned empty-handed.
Within a few days, he died of internal distress. Only one daughter remained, who had already married into the Wu family at Shangshan.
When the daughter returned to escort his coffin for burial, she suddenly beheld her father’s spirit on the road. The spirit then entered her body and returned home, cursing him, saying:

"Tianming was utterly devoid of human sentiment; he caused me to die of suppressed grief. I have now lodged a complaint with the King of the Netherworld and have also informed the local village covenant."
Zonghan has provided testimony. Furthermore, while at the banks of the River in Hangzhou, I encountered my late nephew, Cheng Kuan.
He sent word to me, saying, "I have only this one son; why do you refuse to care for him? Have you given rise to such heterodox thoughts?
Upon hearing this, Xuanwei rebuked him, saying, "During your lifetime, you ruined my family's affairs until they were nearly exhausted."
"Now that I have already died, for what reason do you still come to haunt me? He replied, "In a previous life, I was originally a merchant and you were my shopkeeper.
Seeing my wealth and treasures, you plotted to take my life. I have now come specifically to collect this debt.
However, because you allowed me to spend as I pleased, it greatly gratified my heart; therefore, I spare your life. How can you reproach me with the etiquette due to a father?"
Ah! At the mouth of the Songjiang River, there was a man surnamed Zhu whose habitual occupation was to slaughter large pigs for profit.

During the first month of the Jiumao year of the Chongzhen era, at the second watch, he happened to rise and go to the latrine when he heard the sound of human voices; suspecting them to be thieves, he [investigated].
Holding his staff, he followed the sound and went to investigate; there, inside a pigsty, they were speaking in the Fujian dialect.
One said, "Alas! I shall surely be slaughtered tomorrow. Another said, "By nature you were to be a pig seven times;
now six times have passed, and the suffering is nearly over. As for me, I was to be a pig five times; this is only my first time, which is why it is so painful. Their—
The man originally understood the local dialect of Fujian. Upon hearing this, he was greatly shocked and subsequently abandoned his evil occupation.
There was also another man whose livelihood was slaughtering sheep; in the first month of the year Jia-mao, he traveled to the countryside to purchase four sheep and led them back home.
When they were only about ten *li* away from his house, the four sheep began to struggle and leap about, knocking the man over.
One sheep was led by its head; one sheep pressed down its two hind legs; and two sheep were placed upon its belly, where they struck with all their might until it died.
(The four matters above were recounted because Cheng Zhongyong had personally witnessed them.)
In the Shentiao district, there was once a scholar who attained the jinshi degree at the age of twenty. His presiding examiner and his fellow graduates all held him in high esteem;
yet his father treated him with even greater severity, frequently subjecting him to flogging and humiliation whenever he fell short of his standards.
One day, a fellow graduate invited the scholar to a banquet. Because his father had reprimanded him, the scholar departed late, and upon arriving, he spoke to his fellow graduate.
He wept as he recounted these circumstances. His fellow examinee sighed with great admiration and said, "How extraordinary! Our elder brother has been so deeply supportive of his younger brother.
For while those like us have spent half a lifetime in bitter toil to finally obtain a single degree, you, my brother, achieved that degree before the age of twenty;
moreover, your reputation is already widespread and surpasses ours. This is what the Creator fears. If our elder brother..."

"If you do not employ the harsh tongs and hammers [of discipline], your brother will surely indulge his passions and follow his own whims; thus both his fortune and his longevity will be diminished. The scholar then awakened to the truth.
Upon returning home, he immediately changed his former ways. His father asked him in astonishment, "Did you understand my meaning yourself and thus reform your faults in this way?
Or did someone explain it to you? The scholar replied by recounting the words of his fellow official. Thereupon, his father—

He respectfully invited his peers; the Duke commanded that they be treated with the rites due to scholars and served as teachers, so that he might receive their benefit through mutual correction, polishing, and refinement.
In Hezhou there was a resident whose surname has been forgotten; he raised over a hundred geese. One day, by chance, the geese ate the rice of his neighbors.
The neighbors beat and killed more than fifty of the geese. When the man’s wife saw this, she was initially also very [indignant].

She was angry. She then reflected deeply, saying: "If I were to engage in a lawsuit with him, although my strength would suffice to defeat him, it would require an expenditure of several tens of gold coins.
Calculating the value of the goose, it does not even reach half that amount. Furthermore, even if the goose were dead, it could still be put to use;
why must I struggle over this empty air? Moreover, my husband is now lying drunk; if I were to inform him, he might wake up and beat me. It was even more so...
"It is inconvenient," she said. She then ordered her servant to collect the dead goose and pickle it. The next morning, a neighbor suddenly died of his own accord.
When the husband woke from his drunken stupor, he sighed in astonishment at how the man had passed away without any illness, finding it most extraordinary.
His wife then told him what had happened the previous day. He was deeply moved and said, "If you had told me yesterday, I would have used all my strength while intoxicated to beat him to death."
"Could this not save human lives? He then gathered his relatives and friends to serve as witnesses, prostrating himself to thank his wife (the above two matters explain Cheng Tai’s account).
At the Yijiahuai brokerage house in Chizhou Prefecture, there was a cotton merchant who went to the countryside to collect cotton.
On the way, he encountered a dog-handler carrying a large dog; he purchased it and released it for its life, providing leftover food to feed it. The dog never left his side. One day—
When the day arrived, they went to Dingjiazhou to collect the flowers. The boatman who was acting as their host called for a boat to transport them; the dog also followed along.
Seeing that the guests possessed much silver, the boatman conceived an evil intent. He rowed to the riverbank, placed the guests inside a cloth bag, tied its mouth shut, and threw it into the water.
The dog then leapt into the water, bit through the knot of the bag, and barked incessantly. A fisherman saw this and pulled it out.
The guest consequently regained consciousness and returned to the marketplace, where he recounted the matter in detail.
The master of the market consoled the guest’s mind and feigned ignorance, yet went to the boatman’s house to inquire. The guest then invited the boatman to the market to drink wine;
once there, he ordered the guest to confront him face-to-face, leading the boatman to confess his guilt and return the original silver.
At Mount Jiuhua, there was a man who lived in a village and took pleasure in killing deer. One day, leading his followers, he set a net to catch them.
He saw an old deer with a coat of unusual colors; as he and his men surrounded it, the deer, seeing its situation was desperate, fled into the village house. The group pursued it further.
The deer knelt and prostrated itself, shedding tears as it begged for its life. The hunter pierced the deer’s eye with his spear;
before the hide had even been removed, the hunter’s own eyes suddenly went blind.
In the Lao-tian Wu-liu household of Qingyang County, there was a family member named Wu Mao who maintained the precepts and consumed only vegetarian food with great purity.
When the left-wing troops crossed the river to plunder and kill, the master of the house fled entirely to avoid them; only Wu Mao remained to guard the residence on behalf of his master.
He was struck by seven spear thrusts from the bandits and died. A short while later, his younger brother came to visit him, and Mao revived, speaking to his brother.

He said, "By the force of my past karma, I was destined to undergo seven births as a pig. By the power of my current fasting and precepts, I have now received these seven spears to repay my former causes and shall be reborn directly in heaven.

Having finished speaking, he passed away. His younger brother, who had never before believed in the wholesome, was struck with awe upon hearing this and likewise turned his heart back toward the Dharma.
The mountain streams of Jiuhua Mountain abound with stone chickens; they resemble frogs but are larger, and their flavor surpasses that of domestic fowl.

Whenever a superior official passes through the county, he invariably issues a warrant to seize them. Once, one night, a villager used a torch to illuminate a cliff and reached his hand in to grab one, only to have it bite both his hands so firmly that he could not pull it out and died.
It was not until the fifth watch that he heard the sound of temple bells.
The stone chickens each appeared to be in the posture of joining their palms in recitation of the Buddha’s name. The village headman was thus able to escape.
In Chizhou Prefecture, there was a man who constantly recited the *Sanguan jing*. When bandits approached the city walls, the man dreamed that the Three Officials told him:
"In a previous life, you once killed a person; they have now come to seek revenge, and it cannot be avoided. He was struck with terror and fear.
He awoke and prayed with renewed earnestness. Again he received a dream, which said: "Past karma is difficult to escape; how could it be saved through mere expediency?
However, your former creditor, named Zhu Qi, rides a red horse and will surely come tomorrow.
You should kneel before the gate and cry out, 'General Zhu Qi, spare my life! Should he ask you why you know his name, you must tell him of the two dreams."
This was appropriate. The following day, he indeed saw before the gate one riding a red horse, who knelt and cried out, "General Zhu Qi, spare my life!
When the rebel heard this, he was struck with wonder and asked how it had come to pass. He then looked dejected as if he had lost something, let him go without killing him, and departed.
Shi Fuli was visiting friends when he returned to Jiuhua. That night, he dreamed of three men wearing yellow caps and feathered robes who were fleeing for their lives;
beside them stood a man in similar attire who reviled them. The following day, while traveling on the road, he saw a boy holding three eels, which were exceptionally large and fat.
He purchased them and released them into a well. Beside him stood another monk who scolded him bitterly, saying it was improper to release them there.
At the well, he finally realized that the three eels in his night dream were these very ones. (The above six matters are all based on the account of Shi Longren.
Cheng Boshen, a merchant from Huizhou who had long resided in Yangzhou, served Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva with great devotion.

In the summer of the year Yiyou, when the Northern Army breached the city of Yangzhou, Cheng prayed to the Bodhisattva for rescue. He then received a dream in which it was said: "In your household, there are ten..."
"Seven people; the remaining sixteen souls shall all not undergo this kalpa, but you alone are included in their number—it cannot be avoided.
When Cheng awoke, he again offered earnest prayers, and once more received a dream in which it was said: "In your previous life, you killed King Mazi with twenty-six sword-strokes."
"Now you must repay him; there is absolutely no way to escape.

You should assign the sixteen members of your household to live in the eastern wing, while you alone remain in the central hall to await him. Do not involve your family members in this misfortune. Cheng assented.
Five days later, the northern troops knocked at the door. Cheng immediately asked, "Are you not Wang Mazhi? If you are indeed Wang Mazhi—"
"Come and kill me with twenty-six strokes of the blade; if it were not for Wang Mazzi, there would have been no cause for enmity at all.
There is no need to enter the gate. The soldier said, "I am indeed Wang Mazzi. Cheng then opened the gate and let him in. As the soldier dismounted, he asked in alarm:
"How do you know my name? Cheng told him everything about his two dreams. The soldier sighed and said, "In your previous life, you struck me twenty-six times with a blade.
I am now repaying you in this life. If I kill you now, will you not strike me again in a future life?
He then struck Cheng twenty-six times with the back of his blade and then released him, taking him along.
His family members also arrived together in Jinling.
*Jianwen lu* (end).
